unit: per job: remove the engine oil pan, clean the sealing surfaces and seal it again. What the 'gasket' is depends on the engine and is stated per class: a formed gasket (economy and midsize aftermarket sets), factory liquid sealant in place of a gasket (many four-cylinder engines, including the midsize example at the dealer), or a new pan that carries its own seal (the truck and luxury examples, where the maker's repair is a new pan). All four classes price the LOWER pan on engines where the pan comes off with the engine in the car. Not included: an upper oil pan (the cast aluminum section some engines have between the block and the lower pan), which is a much bigger job; on Subaru flat-four engines the maker's upper-pan reseal starts with taking the engine out. Also not included: lowering a front subframe or removing a front axle, which some rear-drive and four-wheel-drive vehicles need before the pan will come off, and engine oil and filter (see extras)

finding: The live range of $260-$950 is about right for the ordinary case and too low at the top for the hard ones. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks, before engine oil and filter): economy 2015 Corolla, a $10.44 gasket + 1.3-1.5 hr = about $166-$250 (the high side of the parts is null, so this total uses the one gasket price found); midsize 2012 Kia Sportage 2.4L, $26.69-$60.45 + 1.3-2.8 hr = about $183-$508; truck 2016 F-150 2.7L (new pan), $134.00-$209.99 + 3.2-4.1 hr = about $518-$866; luxury 2017 Lincoln MKZ 3.0L (new pan), $131.07-$193.33 + 3.1-3.2 hr = about $503-$705. Add roughly the price of an oil change to each, because the oil has to be drained. The bottom: our lowest totals ($166-$183) sit under the live $260, but they rest on a dealer warranty time of 1.3 hours, which is less than a shop normally bills, and every benchmark starts higher (YourMechanic about $219, Jerry $500, RepairPal $583), so $260 is a fair floor and if anything a little low for a shop. The top: $950 covers every example here, but it does not cover engines where more than the lower pan has to come off. Subaru's own bulletin for an upper oil pan reseal on 2012-2019 Forester and Impreza (02-131-12R) lists engine removal at 3.4-3.9 hours plus 2.4 hours for the reseal, about 5.8-6.3 hours, and its upper-pan replacement bulletin (02-166-17R) lists 5.5-7.1 hours; at $120-$160 an hour that is roughly $660-$1,140 in labor alone. Jerry's guide puts 4WD trucks at 5-8 hours and its top figure is $1,600+. So vehicles that need the engine out, a subframe lowered or a front axle removed can run well past $950. What is null and why: the economy high parts figure. The Toyota dealer catalog lists no engine oil pan gasket for the 2015 Corolla (its gasket page shows only the transaxle pan gasket, and its oil pan page shows the pan and a drain plug washer), which suggests the factory seal is liquid sealant, but no page that loaded confirms that or names the sealant for this engine. Toyota's own oil pan sealant (FIPG, 00295-00103) lists at $25.95, yet other catalogs tie that number to 1990s-2006 models, so it was not used; if it were, the economy top would be about $266, a difference of about $16. How solid the labor times are: the midsize low (1.3 hr), both truck figures (3.2 and 4.1 hr) and the luxury 3.2 hr are manufacturer warranty times for the example vehicles themselves; warranty times are the low end of what shops bill, and the truck and luxury times are for fitting a new pan, which is the same removal and refitting work as a reseal. The economy figures are weaker: the low is the Kia time borrowed for a comparable car and the high is a named mechanic's general statement. The midsize high is a customer estimate for a different car. Three of the eight hour figures are not for the example vehicle. Parts sourcing is thin for economy (one priced page for the example car); midsize now has two priced pages that agree on the $60.45 list price, plus a second aftermarket gasket at $19.54 as a cross-check. The null and the borrowed hours keep confidence low. No stated time was found for a rear-wheel-drive BMW, where the job is known to be bigger; YourMechanic's 328i average of $588 with $490 labor is the only figure loaded for it. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote almost always adds engine oil and a new oil filter, because the oil must be drained to take the pan off. It often adds a diagnosis or dye test to confirm the pan is the source of the leak (valve cover, timing cover and rear main seal leaks run down to the pan and look the same), shop supplies, and sales tax. Possible related parts: new pan bolts where they are single-use (some BMW engines), an oil pump pickup seal or O-rings, an oil level sensor seal, a new drain plug washer, and a new oil pan if the old one is bent, corroded or has stripped threads. On vehicles where a subframe or front axle comes down, a wheel alignment may be added.
